highlights.title: Scheduled Claude Code Routines — Personal Automation Suite
highlights.summary: Four Claude Code cloud routines I wrote that run unattended on a daily schedule and deliver a finished result with no supervision: a two-account inbox digest, a next-day calendar briefing, a Canvas-to-monday.com school-task sync, and a US-market after-close recap email. Each is built to survive missed runs and a stateless sandbox — recovering its own history, resolving its own date in Pacific time, and always sending something so a silent failure stays visible.
metrics: 4 routines on daily/weekday cron: inbox summary (two Gmail accounts, spam included), next-day schedule (three calendars merged and deduped), school-tasks sync (Canvas events into a monday.com board, one group per class), and a US-market after-close recap (indices, top movers, top-10 Nasdaq by market cap, BTC/ETH, upcoming splits and IPOs, earnings calendar, fed/state watch)

Stateless-sandbox persistence, three ways: none for the digests, an external system of record for the sync (the monday.com board, with archived-item lookup so completed items aren't recreated every run), and a machine-readable STATE line embedded in each sent recap that the next run parses back out of sent mail
Missed-run resilience: each routine resolves "today" in Pacific time from a UTC sandbox clock, rolls weekends back to the last trading day, and backfills up to 10 missed weekdays oldest-first

Hardening: inbound mail treated as untrusted data and never as instructions (prompt-injection defense); UTC-to-Pacific conversion before taking a calendar date so due dates don't land a day late; Gmail-safe rendering as colored monospace text bars because Gmail strips images and background-only divs; mandatory post-send integrity check with a one-corrected-resend cap
Always-send contract — every routine emails even on a zero-result run, because a silent run is indistinguishable from a broken one

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 1: Measurements & Uncertainties
highlights.summary: First PHYS 2A lab, on measurement and uncertainty. Uses the method of similar triangles to measure a large object indirectly from a string, a stick of known length, and eye-to-object distances, then compares that against a direct tape measurement. Propagates the individual uncertainties into a total percent uncertainty and reflects on the largest error sources.
metrics: Indirect (similar-triangles) measurement compared to a direct measurement — the estimate landed about 29.9 cm off
Total propagated uncertainty of roughly 13.9% from three sources: baseline, stick, and string measurements
Reflection identifies fixes — finer markings, repeated trials with averaging, measuring in daylight

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 2: 1-D Motion
highlights.summary: One-dimensional motion lab using a wireless Smart Cart on a track with a hanging mass over a pulley. Records position, velocity, and acceleration versus time in PASCO Capstone, fits a constant-acceleration model, and examines how measurement error propagates into the results. Closes on the advantages and limits of mathematical models — good for prediction and analysis, but blind to unmodeled forces and dependent on data quality.
metrics: Constant-acceleration motion measured with a Smart Cart and analyzed against a kinematic model in PASCO Capstone
Discusses error propagation and the trade-offs of mathematical modeling — assumed-constant forces, sensitivity to poor data

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 3: Projectile Motion
highlights.summary: Projectile-motion lab predicting where a spring-gun projectile will land. Measures the launch speed with a photogate, uses kinematics to predict the range, then fires onto carbon paper to compare predicted and actual landing points. Analyzes the outcome in terms of accuracy versus precision and random versus systematic error. Includes the group's data spreadsheet as an appendix.
metrics: Photogate launch speed to kinematic range prediction to carbon-paper landing test
Statistical analysis — mean, standard deviation of the mean, standard error — separating random from systematic error
Finding: precise but not accurate; systematic error and Capstone data failures shifted the whole cluster off target

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 4: Newton's Second Law
highlights.summary: Newton's second law lab relating net force to acceleration with a cart, force sensor, and hanging-mass system on a track. Experiment 1 varies the hanging weight and measures the cart's acceleration; the planned Experiment 2 (acceleration versus cart mass) was designed and predicted analytically but not run for lack of time. Includes the group's data spreadsheet as an appendix.
metrics: Experiment 1: net force versus acceleration measured across seven hanging-mass values with a force sensor and PASCO Capstone
Experiment 2 (a vs. m) planned and predicted (inverse proportionality from a = F/m) but not collected — noted as a time constraint

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 5: Friction
highlights.summary: Friction lab on an inclined plane and a horizontal surface. Draws free-body diagrams, applies Newton's first law, and uses a force sensor with PASCO Capstone to record a force-versus-time curve while pulling a block from rest into motion — identifying the static region, the point of maximum static friction, and the kinetic-friction region. Includes the group's data spreadsheet as an appendix.
metrics: Free-body analysis plus a Capstone force-versus-time trace marking static, maximum-static, and kinetic-friction regions
Static and kinetic friction characterized from inclined-plane and tabletop trials

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 6: Twirly Bob (Circular Motion)
highlights.summary: 'Twirly bob' lab on uniform circular motion and centripetal force. Swings a mass on a string in a horizontal circle (hard hat and goggles required), draws free-body diagrams for the bob and its hanging counterweight, and applies Newton's laws to compute the centripetal acceleration and the force keeping the bob on its circular path, then compares against measured data. Includes the group's data spreadsheet as an appendix.
metrics: Centripetal acceleration and force computed from period, radius, and mass, with free-body diagrams for each mass in the system
The group's first lab turning circular-motion observations into analyzed data; reflection traces outliers to the spinning mass drifting downward

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 7: Rotating Penny
highlights.summary: Circular-motion lab studying a penny on a turntable undergoing non-uniform (angular-accelerating) rotation. Applies Newton's laws to the forces on the penny — normal, gravity, and friction — and splits friction into a radial component that changes direction and a tangential component that changes speed. Measures angular acceleration from the position, velocity, and acceleration graphs and derives when the penny slips. Includes the group's data spreadsheet as an appendix.
metrics: Angular position, velocity, and acceleration graphs read and compared to their linear x/v/a analogues from kinematics
Sliding condition derived: the penny slips once the required friction exceeds maximum static friction, at which point net force and acceleration become nonzero

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 8: Work and Energy
highlights.summary: Work-and-energy lab on an air track: a cart is pulled by a hanging mass over a near-frictionless pulley and, in a second experiment, launched by a compressed spring. Uses work-energy relationships to predict the cart's speed, then cross-checks the spring constant found from the launch against a direct force-sensor measurement. Report only — the data spreadsheet in the source folder is corrupted.
metrics: Cart speed predicted with the work-energy theorem and compared against a Newton's-second-law approach
Spring constant from the launch (1.11) vs. the force-sensor value (1.15) — a 3.4% difference; the force sensor is trusted more for excluding external forces

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 10: Rotational Equilibrium
highlights.summary: Statics and torque lab done ahead of the CH9 unit. Balances a meter stick on a pivot with clamped masses to predict an unknown mass from rotational equilibrium — locating the stick's center of mass, then solving the sum-of-torques and sum-of-forces equations. No sensors; measurements taken with error bars and analyzed by hand. Includes the group's data spreadsheet as an appendix.
metrics: Unknown mass predicted from a torque-balance equation using the meter stick's mass, its center of mass, and two known masses' positions
Explains why the pivot's normal force drops out of the torque calculation, with extended free-body diagrams showing action/reaction pairs

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 11: Rotational Inertia
highlights.summary: Rotational-inertia lab: a horizontal rod with two movable masses is spun by a falling hanging mass while PASCO Capstone records angular acceleration, which is used to compute the system's rotational inertia. Varies how far the masses sit from the rotation axis and compares the experimental results against a theoretical model. Includes the group's data spreadsheet as an appendix.
metrics: Rotational inertia determined from measured angular acceleration for several mass positions; I-vs-r shows a linear best fit — resistance to rotation rises as mass moves outward
Sample calculations for net force, tension, net torque, and rotational inertia; discusses extending the setup to test energy conservation (Mgh = 1/2 mv^2 + 1/2 Iw^2)

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Lab 13: Temperature, Pressure, Density & Buoyancy
highlights.summary: Four-station exploratory lab on the thermal and physical properties of materials and water — temperature, pressure, density, and buoyancy. Stations include a vapor-pressure flask demonstration and hot-vs-ice-water comparisons, with written analysis connecting results to reduced boiling point at altitude and Archimedes' water-displacement method for testing density. Includes the group's data spreadsheet as an appendix.
metrics: Four rotating stations, roughly 30-45 minutes each, with measurements and observations recorded per station
Applied questions — why rice cooks slower at altitude (lower atmospheric pressure lowers the boiling point), and Archimedes' displacement test of King Hiero's crown

highlights.title: PHYS 2A — Practicum 4: Newton's Second Law
highlights.summary: Individual practicum (practical exam) on Newton's second law — the same cart, force-sensor, and hanging-mass setup as Lab 4, run and analyzed solo. A spreadsheet records mass, weight, applied force, and measured acceleration across trials to check the net-force and acceleration relationship.
metrics: Solo assessment: mass, weight, applied force, and acceleration recorded and analyzed per trial
Checks the linear net-force vs. acceleration relationship (a = F/m) from the individual data
